text: The last three lessons covered three separate ideas on their own: scripts live in Git, pipelines run them on a hosted machine instead of a laptop, and credentials come from the pipeline's own secret store, never typed into a file. A real pipeline uses all three of those ideas at once, and this lesson walks through exactly one complete example, end to end, line by line.

This workflow runs the VM start and stop script from Lesson 21, automatically, every weeknight, in four steps: a trigger fires the job on a schedule with no laptop required, a checkout step pulls the repository's script onto a hosted runner, a login step authenticates using a stored secret that's never written into this file, and a run step executes the exact same script, with the full run logged automatically.

on: schedule: with cron: "0 23 * * MON-FRI" fires this job at 23:00 UTC every weeknight, exactly the reliable, unattended trigger from Lesson 26, and workflow_dispatch adds a manual override. actions/checkout@v4 matters because a hosted runner starts completely empty — this step is what pulls scripts/Stop-DevVMs.ps1 onto that machine in the first place.

azure/login@v2 is the authentication step, and it's where Lesson 27 matters directly: creds: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CREDENTIALS }} pulls a service principal credential from the repository's GitHub Actions secrets, never from plain text in this file, and logs the runner into Azure for the rest of the job. With the repo checked out and the runner authenticated, ./scripts/Stop-DevVMs.ps1 then runs on a consistent hosted image.

Nothing here is a toy example — swap Stop-DevVMs.ps1 for the tag-compliance script from Lesson 22 or the backup-verification script from Lesson 23, and the same four steps still apply: trigger, checkout, login, run. Next up: Chapter 8's lab, building a cost-savings automation script and wiring it into a pipeline exactly like this one.
